narrative:
The model predicted a 65% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the second decile, noticeably lower than the average of roughly sixth-decile performance among students who were accepted. Your first-year ranking was the third most important factor and also worked against you, landing in the third decile compared with an average around the sixth decile for admitted students.

Your LSAT score was the second most influential piece of information, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 39, your score sits above the 37.2 average of accepted students and therefore pulled the prediction toward passing. Unfortunately, this positive signal was not large enough to overcome the negative impact of your class rankings.

You should focus on strengthening your academic performance and class standing in the coming semesters. Improving your position in the upper half of your class would likely shift future predictions in your favor and improve your chances of admission. Consider speaking with an academic advisor about targeted steps to raise your rankings before reapplying.
